name: gemdb
description: Python with built-in transactional persistence (using true ACID semantics). When you have critical, complex data that must be consistent, use GemDB.

untrustedWorkspaces.description: GemDB's status, setup and database controls work in Restricted Mode. Running Python from this folder (notebook cells, Run File, the GemDB Shell) waits until you trust it, and VS Code asks you when you first try.

gemdb.rootPath.markdownDescription: Directory that holds the GemDB database engine and your database. It must be on a local disk: the database engine will not open its files on an NFS mount, and a folder that iCloud Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox or a similar service syncs will corrupt a live database. GemDB does not move anything when this changes; run **Set Up GemDB** afterwards to set up the new location.

gemdb.engineVersion.markdownDescription: Advanced: override the pinned database engine version (e.g. `4.0.0.a4`). Leave empty to use the version this release of GemDB Code was built and tested against. A version that is not published at dl.gemdb.com cannot be downloaded — it must already be present under the root path.

gemdb.reinstallPythonOnUpdate.description: When a GemDB Code update ships a newer Python execution engine, reinstall it into your database automatically the next time GemDB Code starts.

gemdb.mcp.enabled.markdownDescription:
Run GemDB's **MCP server**, so AI agents can query and change your database. It starts and stops with the database, listens on `127.0.0.1` only, and is registered with this editor automatically. Run **GemDB: Connect an AI Agent to GemDB** for the configuration other clients need.

**Off by default while a session-accounting limitation is fixed upstream.** Each connected client is given its own database session, and one is not released until the client disconnects cleanly or 30 minutes pass — so a client that repeatedly reconnects or crashes can use up the limited number of sessions the database allows, and lock you out of it until they are reaped. Turn this on if you want agent access now; the GemDB panel shows what is connected.

gemdb.mcp.port.markdownDescription: Port the MCP server listens on, always bound to `127.0.0.1`. Deliberately not `8000` — that is what most development servers take, and the MCP server refuses a port already in use. Changing this needs **GemDB: Restart the MCP Server**, and every client configured with the old URL has to be updated.

gemdb.mcp.readOnly.markdownDescription: Run AI agents as a database user that cannot commit, so an agent can read and run code but nothing it does can be made permanent. Off by default: running Python in your database is most of why you would connect an agent to it. Enforced by GemStone rather than by hiding tools — the first time you turn this on, GemDB creates an `McpReadOnly` user in your database whose profile disables commits. It bounds what an agent can CHANGE, not what it can read or how much of the machine it can use. Changing this restarts the MCP server, which disconnects any connected agent.

gemdb.externalDatabase.gemstone.markdownDescription: Advanced: use a database that someone else installed and runs — a hosted or shared machine — instead of one GemDB Code installs. Set to that engine's product directory (its `GEMSTONE`). GemDB Code then downloads nothing, creates no database, and never starts, stops or removes the database: it only installs Python support into your account and connects. Leave empty for a database GemDB Code manages. The other `gemdb.externalDatabase.*` settings apply only when this is set.

gemdb.externalDatabase.globalDirectory.markdownDescription: The external database's global directory (its `GEMSTONE_GLOBAL_DIR`), which holds the engine's `locks` directory. GemDB Code reads it to find the stone and NetLDI.

gemdb.externalDatabase.stone.markdownDescription: Name of the external database's stone.

gemdb.externalDatabase.netldi.markdownDescription: Name of the external database's NetLDI. It must run in guest mode (`startnetldi -g`), as your operating-system account, so sessions need no host password — and with Python's variables (`GRAIL_DIR`, `PYTHON_PACKAGE_PATH`, `SHIM_LIB_PATH`) set to your GemDB Code root path's `grail` directory, because sessions inherit its environment.

gemdb.externalDatabase.user.markdownDescription: Database account GemDB Code logs in as on the external database. Python support is installed into this account.

gemdb.externalDatabase.passwordFile.markdownDescription: File whose first line is the password for `gemdb.externalDatabase.user`, readable only by your operating-system account. A file rather than a setting, so the password never appears in `settings.json`. Leave empty for the stock password.

walkthroughs.title: Get Started with GemDB Code
walkthroughs.description: Install the database, start it, and run your first Python in it.

steps.title: The automated GemDB setup
steps.description:
GemDB Code downloads the database engine, creates your database, and installs Python into it. If the shared-memory limit is too low, GemDB Code prompts you to raise it. If you canceled setup, click **Set Up GemDB** to continue where it left off.
[Set Up GemDB](command:gemdb.install)

steps.title: Setup for this machine's database
steps.description:
GemDB Code is set to use this machine's database, which its administrator runs. Setup installs Python support into your account. It downloads nothing.
[Set Up GemDB](command:gemdb.install)

steps.title: Run your first Python
steps.description:
Open a Python prompt that runs inside the database. If the database is stopped and GemDB Code runs it, opening the shell starts it.
[Open GemDB Shell](command:gemdb.openRepl)

steps.title: Open a notebook
steps.description:
Create a notebook and run Python inside the database, one cell at a time.
[New GemDB Notebook](command:gemdb.newNotebook)

steps.title: Explore a real application
steps.description:
Brain Freeze is a small web app, built with Flask, whose data, classes, and views are stored in the database. Installing it clones a copy into `~/GemDB/brain-freeze`, opens it, and displays its README.
[Install Brain Freeze Demo](command:gemdb.cloneBrainFreeze)

steps.title: Stopping the database
steps.description:
The database keeps running after you close VS Code, so your data stays available. To stop it, click **GemDB** in the status bar. Commit your work first, because uncommitted changes are discarded.
[Stop GemDB](command:gemdb.stop)

scripts.//lint:toolchain: Asserts the repo's own node_modules/.bin/tsc is TypeScript 7. We have both TS 6 (linter) and TS 7 (typechecks) in the project.
scripts.//hooks: Local git hooks (lefthook.yml): eslint + prettier on staged files, and a non-blocking package-lock.json warning after checkout/merge/rebase. lefthook's postinstall installs them on `npm install`, so use hooks:uninstall to opt out. CI's `checks` job is the gate regardless.
scripts.//package: Platform-specific builds: each .vsix carries the CPython shim for one platform, so the Marketplace offers each machine only the build that can work on it. `package` builds the target matching this machine; `package:all` needs every platform's shim staged in grail/prebuilt (see CONTRIBUTING.md).
scripts.//publish: The release pipeline (.github/workflows/release.yml) is how a release is published; these are the manual fallback and what it is built from. Both publish the packages CI built and tested, collected into dist/ by `npm run release:fetch`. Neither repackages: no single machine can build all three shims, so a local rebuild would be a different artifact from the one that passed.
scripts.publish: npm run publish:vsce && npm run publish:ovsx
